note: py_module/py_scope/py_binding emitted in frozen column order (24/25/29). Stage-2 entity models and enums also landed (py_type 25, py_type_base 16, py_method 36, py_method_parameter 22, py_import 24) but are NOT yet populated by an extractor.

subject: scopeOrdinal is evaluation order, not source order
detail: symtable orders a block's children by CONSTRUCTION order. Signature parts are evaluated before the body exists, so in `def __init__(self, spec=lambda: 1)` the lambda is a SIBLING built first: lambda=ordinal 0, method=ordinal 1, even though the def starts at an earlier column. Sorting children by (line,column) inverts them. Affected 260 scope rows across the stdlib sweep. Now mirrors symtable.c exactly: defaults, kw_defaults, annotations (posonly, args, vararg, kwarg, kwonly, returns), decorators, body.

subject: symtable visits try/else BEFORE except handlers
detail: CPython's symtable.c Try_kind visits body, then orelse, then handlers, then finalbody — not source order, and not the order the compiler uses. locale.py depends on it: its two conditional getpreferredencoding defs (lines 652 and 657) get ordinals 30 and 29 respectively.

subject: symtable.py decides module scope by NAME, not block type
detail: symtable.py does `module_scope = (self._table.name == "top")`, so ANY function or class literally named `top` receives module-scope semantics for is_local/is_global — a bound name reports both. Reproduced deliberately because symtable is the oracle. Real case: poplib.POP3.top reports its parameters as is_global=true. Flagging as a CPython wart the engine may want to know about rather than a parser choice.

subject: PEP 563 suppresses annotation visits entirely
detail: Under `from __future__ import annotations`, CPython 3.10 does not visit annotation expressions at all, so a TYPE_CHECKING-only import used solely in a signature is is_referenced=false. Without the future import the same name is is_referenced=true. Verified both directions. Consequence for the engine: is_referenced cannot be used to decide whether an import is live when futureImports contains `annotations`.

subject: tree-sitter parse ceiling confirmed at exactly 32767 characters
detail: Measured against tree-sitter 0.21.1 / tree-sitter-python 0.21.0: a 32,767-character buffer parses, 32,768 throws `Invalid argument`. Characters, not bytes — 29,007 chars of CJK (87,007 UTF-8 bytes) parses fine. PythonParser streams in 8KB chunks above 30,000 chars, mirroring java-parser.ts:43. Files are never split, so there is always exactly one root and module containment is intact.

subject: Python 2 three-tier detection verified against the grammar
detail: Tier 1 node types (print_statement, exec_statement, chevron) all parse with hasError=false, confirming rejection cannot rely on parse failure. Tier 2 shapes verified distinguishable: `except E, e:` has a direct comma child where `except E as e:` produces an as_pattern, and a Py2 tuple parameter is a tuple_pattern whose PARENT is `parameters`/`lambda_parameters` where the legal Py3 `(a,b) = x` has parent `assignment`. Tier 3 backticks confirmed indistinguishable in the tree (string/string_start/string_content/string_end, hasError=false), so a raw-source scan is required; the scan tracks string and comment state so backticks in docstrings and comments do not cause false rejections. 15/15 detector cases pass, including 9 negative Py3 cases.

subject: emissionRegime PY3_12_PLUS currently refuses rather than emits
detail: The extractor throws when emissionRegime != PY3_0_11. Rationale: the 3.12 regime differs structurally at every list/set/dict comprehension (PEP 709), the pinned oracle is 3.10.4 and refuses to run under any other interpreter, so emitting 3.12 facts would produce rows nothing can adjudicate. Refusing seemed better than guessing. Confirm that is the behaviour you want, or tell me to implement the subtractive gate unverified.

implement the gate now, marked unverified

subject: nonlocal with no binding in any enclosing scope
detail: `nonlocal x` where no enclosing scope binds x is a SyntaxError in CPython, so symtable never produces a fact set for such a file and the oracle cannot adjudicate it. The parser currently records the declared intent (a NONLOCAL binding with scope FREE and no target) rather than rejecting the file, on the grounds that rejecting loses every other fact in it. Escalating per brief: this is a question about what the reasoning engine needs, not a parser decision.

subject: star-import expansion remains unexpanded
detail: `from x import *` sets py_scope.usesWildcardImport and emits one py_import row with isWildcard=true, binding no names. The parser does not expand it even when the target module is in the repo and its __all__ is static. Per brief this is a your-call item: expanding would invent bindings symtable does not have (so the oracle would report them as spurious), while not expanding leaves a known soundness hole the engine must handle. 22 sites in the measured corpus.

subject: py_method_parameter.position ordering — parser vs oracle ast dump
detail: Gate 2 disagreement, resolved in the parser's favour with third-party evidence. For `def full_signature(a, b, /, c, d=10, *args, e, f=20, **kwargs)` the oracle's ast dump lists params grouped (posonlyargs, args, kwonlyargs, then vararg, then kwarg) giving a,b,c,d,e,f,args,kwargs; the parser emits canonical signature order a,b,c,d,args,e,f,kwargs. CPython's own inspect.signature reports the parser's order exactly. This matters rather than being cosmetic: positional argument flow indexes on `position`, so placing KEYWORD_ONLY params at indices 4-5 ahead of *args at 6 would let a rule bind a 5th positional argument to `e`, which can never receive one. All paramKind values agreed; only the sequence differed. Parser unchanged; the differential checker now compares parameters as a set of name:kind pairs. Flagging in case A0 wants the ast dump reordered so the two agree positionally.

subject: isGenerator — oracle's _has_yield walks into nested functions
detail: The oracle's ast-side helper `_has_yield` returns true when ANY descendant contains a yield, including inside a nested def, so it reports isGenerator=true for a function that merely RETURNS a generator. CPython disagrees with the oracle here: inspect.isgeneratorfunction is False for concurrent.futures._base.Executor.map, asyncio.coroutines.coroutine and ctypes.macholib.dyld.dyld_image_suffix_search, all three of which the oracle marks as generators. The parser stops at nested def/class boundaries and reports false, matching CPython. Note the helper has the same dead-code shape as `_declares` (a `continue` that does nothing, then a final unconditional ast.walk), so both may be worth a look. Parser unchanged; the differential checker now skips isGenerator for functions that contain a nested def, so real regressions are still caught elsewhere.
suggestedOracleFix: restrict _has_yield to the function's own body, and consider the same for _declares

note: All 10 frozen spine relations (262 columns) now emit. Byte-identical across runs for the full 10-relation output.

subject: receiverKind — the oracle's visit_Call ignores decorators entirely
detail: Two remaining sweep disagreements, both from the same root cause in the oracle's ast-side visit_Call: it computes `selfn = first_param_name if (first and self.cls)` and then tests `SELF if b.id == selfn else (CLS if b.id == 'cls' else NAME)`, which (a) never consults the decorator list and (b) string-matches the literal name 'cls'. Consequences: `@staticmethod def _interpolation_replace(match, parser)` calling `match.group(1)` is reported SELF (configparser.py:553,555) although a staticmethod has no receiver at all; and module-level `def __newobj__(cls, *args): return cls.__new__(cls, *args)` is reported CLS (copyreg.py:101,107) although it is a plain function parameter that merely happens to be named cls. The parser reports NAME for both, which is what the code says. Note the parser DOES report CLS for a genuine @classmethod, where the oracle reports SELF because its SELF test fires first — so the two disagree in both directions from one bug. Parser unchanged; differential checker exempts these shapes.
evidence: configparser.py:553,555 and copyreg.py:101,107 under the pinned 3.10.4
suggestedOracleFix: consult decorator_list before classifying the receiver, and drop the literal 'cls' string match

subject: keywordNames ordering and literal receivers
detail: Two more resolved in the parser's favour. (1) keywordNames: schema §2.16 c15 specifies SOURCE order; the oracle emits it alphabetically sorted. Source order is the contract and is also what argument flow needs. (2) A literal receiver such as "a,b".split(",") is reported UNKNOWN by the oracle; LITERAL is an explicit schema value (§2.16 c4) and strictly more informative. Both compared as sets / exempted in the checker rather than changed in the parser.

subject: six expression-stage drops found only by sweeping real code
detail: Each of these silently discarded facts and none was caught by the 18 fixtures. (1) A dict literal's children are `pair` nodes; dropping unrecognised nodes discarded every key and value in every dict, including calls — _strptime.py has six. Root cause was the design of the unknown-node path, so unrecognised nodes are now TRANSPARENT rather than dropped: worst case is a flatter tree, never a missing fact. (2) `d[a, b, c]` has three `subscript` field children and childForFieldName returns only the first, losing every index after the first (dataclasses.py:1081-1084). (3) An f-string inside an IMPLICIT concatenation — `f'{type(x)}' 'more text'` — parses to concatenated_string, which was treated as a literal leaf, so its interpolations and their calls vanished; common in error-message construction. (4) A sole generator-expression argument has NO argument_list wrapper, so its element and for-clauses were counted as separate positional arguments and calls inside the clause were lost. (5) `comment` is a named node and can sit between arguments, inflating positionalArgCount on commented multi-line calls. (6) Lambda parameter defaults are evaluated in the enclosing scope and were not walked at all (`lambda x=Nasty(): None`). Also fixed: expressionKindOf was enqueueing work AND returning null, so the transparent fallback re-enqueued the same node and every annotation sub-expression was emitted twice with an identical PK — classification is now documented as pure.

subject: A2 findings in manifest-native.jsonl
detail: Read all four open findings. typeCategory_classification (line 22, high, A3+A0) is mine and is accepted — the metaclass=ABCMeta / metaclass=EnumMeta idiom is currently misclassified because classifyType only inspects positional bases, not keyword arguments. Fixing next. The other three are A0's: comprehension_pairing (critical, oracle mis-pairs same-line nested comprehensions), parenthesized_list_splat and union_type (both unfixturable in the pinned grammar). I have not touched the oracle or staging fixtures, per boundaries. Will flip status by appending a resolution row referencing the same construct rather than editing A2's rows.

Accepted and fixed exactly as diagnosed. classifyType() now inspects the metaclass= keyword value with the same equality tests it applies to positional bases: metaclass=ABCMeta (and the dotted abc.ABCMeta) yields ABC_TYPE, metaclass=EnumMeta/EnumType yields ENUM_CLASS_TYPE. typeModifiersOf() now filters keyword bases the same way classifyType does and checks the metaclass explicitly, so the two passes can no longer disagree about whether a keyword entry counts — that disagreement was the root cause of the internally inconsistent typeModifier=ABSTRACT + typeCategory=CLASS_TYPE row. All 7 of A2's repro cases now match hand-derived expectations, including the two contrast cases that were already correct.
oracleGapAddressed: A2 is right that neither gate can see this field, so the fix is guarded by a direct assertion test rather than a differential one: src/test/python-scratch/classify-test.ts asserts typeCategory and the ABSTRACT modifier per class AND asserts the internal-consistency invariant that ABSTRACT never coexists with CLASS_TYPE. This is a self-check, not an oracle check — recorded as such. A0 still needs to surface ast.ClassDef.keywords as a metaclass field if these columns are to be oracle-adjudicated.

subject: typeCategory and typeModifier have no oracle coverage at all
detail: Seconding A2's oracle_gap note with a scope question. py_type.typeCategory (c3), typeAccess (c4), typeModifier (c5), typePlacement (c6) and mroKind (c21) are all ast-derivable and therefore Gate-2 territory by the schema's own layer-2 definition, but emit_oracle.py emits none of them and diff-decl compares only endLine and positional baseCount. The same is true of py_method.methodKind/methodModifier and py_import.importKind. These are currently guarded only by my own assertion tests, which share an author with the code under test and so detect regressions but not wrong premises. Worth deciding whether A0 extends the ast dump to cover them, or whether they are accepted as parser-adjudicated with self-tests as the only net.

Reproduced A2's finding from the parser side and confirmed the oracle is wrong, with independent evidence. For `result = [q for q in [r for r in z]]` the oracle attributes binding `r` to the scope at column 9 and `q` to the scope at column 21 — exactly swapped. CPython's own ast settles it: the ListComp at col 9 is `[q for q in [r for r in z]]` and binds q, the ListComp at col 21 is `[r for r in z]` and binds r. The parser emits col 9 -> q, col 21 -> r, i.e. correctly. Mechanism agrees with A2's root_cause: the outer comprehension's outermost iterable is evaluated in the ENCLOSING scope, so the inner comprehension is a SIBLING of the outer one and symtable constructs it FIRST; _pair_children's leftmost-column tie-break then pairs that first symtable child with the leftmost ast node, which is the outer comprehension.
gate1Exposure: Any file with same-line nested comprehensions will produce SPURIOUS Gate-1 binding disagreements, and the failure points at the parser. Confirming for the record that the parser must NOT be changed to match the oracle here. Not hit by my sweeps: the 250-file all-gates sweep and the 10,769-file scope sweep were Gate-1 clean, so the shape is rare in the stdlib — but it is silent when it occurs, which is the dangerous part.
evidence: src/test/python-scratch/nested-comp.py; ast.get_source_segment + generator targets under the pinned 3.10.4
action: no parser change; awaiting A0 fix to _pair_children

subject: Gate 1 across the full local corpus: 10,769 files
detail: Ran the scope/binding differential over every .py in the pinned CPython 3.10.4 stdlib and site-packages. Result: 10,757 files fully clean, 206,344 of 206,354 scopes and 1,449,036 of 1,449,064 bindings matching symtable exactly. Of the 11 files with any disagreement, ALL 11 are the same-line comprehension pairing defect A2 reported (construct comprehension_pairing) — every one is a scopeOrdinal swap plus the binding sets swapping with it. One further file (numpy executor.py) could not be judged because the oracle itself failed to produce output; the test harness now records that as unjudged rather than dying on it. Same signature as the earlier synthetic case.

subject: grammar EXTRAS were counted as call arguments
detail: Line-continuation backslashes and comments inside an argument list are NAMED nodes in tree-sitter, so counting named children inflated positionalArgCount. Both occur in real code — ftplib.py:975 and idlelib/debugger_r.py:362 use a continuation inside the argument list, argparse uses inline comments. Fixed by testing tree-sitter's own `node.isExtra` rather than maintaining a blacklist of node types, and applied at every enqueue site so an extra can never become a phantom expression either. Found by the 1,500-file all-gates sweep; the 18 fixtures do not contain a continuation inside an argument list, which is a genuine fixture gap if A2 wants one.

subject: Full-corpus validation, all three gates: 13,586 files
detail: Ran the complete suite over every .py in the pinned CPython 3.10.4 stdlib and site-packages. 13,480 of 13,586 files fully clean (99.2%). Emitted 310,143 scopes, 2,087,179 bindings, 36,238 types, 276,798 methods, 467,124 parameters, 143,178 imports, 11,018,569 expressions and 1,337,938 call sites. 8 files could not be judged because CPython itself failed to produce ground truth; those are reported separately and never counted as passes. Every remaining disagreement falls into three classes, two of which are oracle-side and one of which is now fixed.

subject: grammar extras were counted as PARAMETERS as well as arguments
detail: Same root cause as the argument-list fix, in a place I had not covered: a comment or line continuation inside a PARAMETER list is a named node, so it was counted as a keyword-only parameter and inflated kwOnlyCount. Real occurrences: aiohttp/web_app.py:105 and web_protocol.py:162 both end a parameter with `debug: Any = ...,  # mypy doesn't support ellipsis`. Fixed by testing isExtra in every parameter iteration across all three extractors, including the receiver-detection path, so a comment before the first parameter cannot make a method look receiver-less. aiohttp is now 45/45 clean on all gates.

subject: CPython 3.10 reports FICTIONAL positions inside multi-line f-strings
detail: Resolved in the parser's favour with direct evidence. On the pinned 3.10.4, ast gives f-string interpolation sub-expressions positions that do not correspond to the source — this is the pre-PEP-701 f-string limitation. Minimal repro: for a line whose actual text is `    Thread: {threading.current_thread().name}`, where `threading` begins at column 13, ast reports the call at col_offset 36. The parser reports 13, the real position. Consequence: the ~14 remaining Gate-3 MISSING/SPURIOUS pairs are the SAME call reported at two different columns, not a missing fact. Keeping real positions is the right call because startColumn is in the py_expression primary key and a span must contain its own text; adopting ast's number would give spans that point at nothing. Real case: idlelib/run.py:415.
evidence: ast under the pinned 3.10.4 vs the source line

detail: Every remaining Gate-1 disagreement in the 13,586-file run is this one defect — there are no others. Two additions to A2's report. (1) It also affects nested LAMBDAS, not just comprehensions: py3_test_grammar.py:364 is `l4 = lambda x = lambda y = lambda z=1 : z : y() : x()`, three lambdas on one line all named `lambda`, where the leftmost-column tie-break cannot match construction order by construction. (2) Further real cases: py3_test_grammar.py:875 `(x for x in (y for y in a))` and :880, and test_generator_nested.py:105 `[Yield([e] + p) for p in perms([x for x in l if x != e])]`. Frequency: 11 files out of 13,586, so rare but silent.

subject: Gate 3 (runtime) — closing the no-oracle gap on typeCategory / typeModifier / methodKind
detail: Built a THIRD adjudicator for the fields no static oracle covers, because a self-test written by the code's own author catches regressions but cannot falsify a wrong premise. It imports the module and interrogates the LIVE OBJECTS with CPython introspection — dataclasses.is_dataclass, inspect.isabstract, inspect.iscoroutinefunction, inspect.isgeneratorfunction, __slots__, __dataclass_params__.frozen, _is_protocol, _is_runtime_protocol. That is different evidence in kind: the runtime knows what a class IS without reading how it was written, so a premise shared between the parser and a static checker cannot hide. Tooling: src/test/python-runtime/probe_runtime.py plus src/test/python-runtime-adjudicator.ts. Result on 366 stdlib modules: 1,307 classes and 436 methods checked, 26 disagreements found, 22 fixed, 4 residual and attributable. LIMITATION, stated plainly: importing executes module-level code, so 34 of 400 files could not be imported and are reported UNJUDGED, never as passes. This is a sampling check, not a corpus-wide gate.
residual: 4 of 1307. Two are cross-module bases (`class BrokenProcessPool(_base.BrokenExecutor)`) which are layer-4 engine work by §0.5. Two are a base bound by assignment to a call result (`_Instruction = collections.namedtuple(...)` then `class Instruction(_Instruction)`), which is constructor-call inference and belongs to the deferred py_type_inference relation. Neither is a defect; both are the documented layer boundary.

subject: typeCategory=CLASS_TYPE emitted alongside an ABSTRACT modifier on real stdlib code
detail: The self-contradictory row A2 predicted was still being produced — my own consistency assertion never fired because it only ever ran on my 7-class fixture, where the shape could not occur. The runtime adjudicator found it on the first real module containing ABCs: numbers.Complex, Real, Rational and Integral each emitted typeCategory=CLASS_TYPE with modifier=ABSTRACT,SLOTS. Cause: those classes inherit ABCMeta through a base rather than naming it, so only the @abstractmethod scan fired, and that scan set the modifier without touching the category. Fixed: a class declaring abstract members in its own body is ABC_TYPE. Purely syntactic — the decorators are in the class body — so no cross-module knowledge is needed. This is the concrete case for why a self-test is not a substitute for an independent authority.

subject: Python's THREE implicit method conversions were not modelled
detail: Python converts three dunders with no decorator written: __new__ becomes a staticmethod, and __init_subclass__ and __class_getitem__ become classmethods. The parser reported __class_getitem__ as DUNDER_METHOD where the runtime reports CLASS_METHOD (found on dataclasses.InitVar). This matters for the same reason a missed @classmethod does: it changes what argument 0 is, and therefore shifts every positional argument→parameter link. Now modelled, with __new__ keeping the more specific ALLOCATOR the schema designates for it.

subject: ABC_TYPE is NOT inherited by subclasses — caught mid-fix
detail: While adding same-module base propagation for typeCategory I initially treated ABC_TYPE as inheritable. The runtime adjudicator immediately rejected that: `class closing(AbstractContextManager)` descends from an ABC and is perfectly concrete, and inspect.isabstract agrees, so nine concrete contextlib classes were mislabelled ABC_TYPE. Abstractness depends on whether abstract methods remain UNIMPLEMENTED, which is per-class. PROTOCOL_TYPE and DATACLASS_TYPE are excluded from inheritance for the same kind of reason: subclassing a Protocol yields an implementation, and @dataclass decorates one class. Worth recording because the adjudicator caught both the original under-claim and my over-correction within the same session — which is the argument for having it.

subject: my own fixture asserted behaviour for code that cannot run
detail: A2's typeCategory repro included `class FunctionalEnum(metaclass=EnumMeta): RED = 1`, which I copied into a self-test. It raises TypeError at import — the Enum machinery needs its own base — so the assertion was about impossible code. Found immediately by trying to import the fixture. Frequency evidence on the underlying rule: across the 13,586-file corpus, metaclass=ABCMeta appears 219 times (A2's ABCMeta half is well justified and runtime-confirmed), while metaclass=EnumMeta/EnumType appears 3 times, of which the only one relying on the metaclass ALONE is the definition of enum.Enum itself — where the rule is correct. Rule kept; fixture corrected to the memberless form, which is what actually occurs.

subject: lambdas were not emitted as py_method at all
detail: Schema §2.7 lists `lambda` alongside `def` and `async def`, names it `<lambda>`, and justifies startColumn's place in the py_method PK entirely by lambdas (`g = (lambda: 1, lambda: 2)` gives two rows identical in name, qualifiedName, signature and startLine). Measured at 369 rows in A0's corpus. They were missing entirely, and three things broke silently as a result: (1) a LAMBDA scope's ownerHash had no py_method to point at, so it was falling back to the enclosing method and — at module level — to the py_module hash, giving a discriminator that says LAMBDA against a hash in the wrong relation; (2) every call inside a lambda body was attributed to the enclosing function, which is a real call-graph error since a lambda is a separately-invocable callable; (3) methodKind=LAMBDA and expressionOwnerKind=LAMBDA were never emitted. Now emitted in a dedicated pass, because lambdas are EXPRESSIONS and the statement walk never reaches those in defaults, decorators, class bases or comprehensions. Verified: `sorted(items, key=lambda item: compute(item.rank))` now attributes `sorted` to the enclosing function and `compute` to the lambda. +55 method rows over 400 stdlib files.

subject: invariant #1 was checking FK non-emptiness, not FK TARGET relation
detail: Appendix B #1 says a polymorphic FK resolves in the relation selected by its discriminator. My check only asserted non-emptiness, so a py_scope with ownerKind=LAMBDA pointing at a py_module PK passed: present, and non-dangling against the union of all PKs. Strengthened to resolve each discriminator against its own relation, and it immediately found a SECOND instance of the same bug — module-level comprehension scopes also pointing at the py_module hash instead of the enclosing method. Both fixed. Recording because the weak version of this check is worse than none: it reads as coverage while permitting exactly the error it names.

subject: decorator coverage — what IS and is NOT emitted
detail: py_decorator is one of the eleven DEFERRED relations, so it is deliberately not emitted, and with it go the decorator's own identity, its arguments, applicationOrder, replacesTarget and builtinKind. What IS captured, because it changes DISPATCH and therefore belongs on the spine: py_method.methodKind distinguishes PROPERTY_GETTER / PROPERTY_SETTER / PROPERTY_DELETER / STATIC_METHOD / CLASS_METHOD / ABSTRACT_METHOD / OVERLOAD_STUB, py_method.methodModifier carries PROPERTY|SETTER|DELETER|STATIC|CLASS|ABSTRACT|OVERLOAD|FINAL|CACHED, decoratorCount is recorded, py_type picks up DATACLASS_TYPE and the FROZEN / FINAL / RUNTIME_CHECKABLE modifiers, and every decorator EXPRESSION is emitted as py_expression with rootContext=DECORATOR and edgeRole=DECORATOR_EXPR, including a py_call_site with callKind=DECORATOR_CALL for a parameterised decorator such as @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None). Verified on a probe covering all of these. The gap to state plainly: an @overload stub and its implementation are correctly distinguished as separate py_method rows, but nothing records that a decorator REPLACES the object it decorates — that is replacesTarget on the deferred py_decorator, so for now the engine must not assume a decorated name still refers to the def.

subject: Traceability — the assumption deferral rests on, verified by traversal
detail: All eleven deferred relations point INTO the spine rather than the reverse (py_decorator carries ownerHash polymorphic by context, pyTypeLinkHash, pyMethodLinkHash, pyExpressionLinkHash and pyModuleLinkHash), so deferral is only safe if those spine PKs exist and the chain from any expression up to its owning method is unbroken. Verified by traversal rather than assertion: 984,092 links across 1,200 stdlib files, 0 broken. Checked paths: py_expression -> owner resolved IN THE RELATION ITS DISCRIMINATOR NAMES -> py_method -> py_module; py_call_site -> py_expression, -> py_method (caller), -> py_type, -> receiver expression; py_method -> scope, type, enclosing member, declaring binding; py_type -> scope, <classbody>, enclosing type, module; and the scope chain terminating at exactly one root with no cycles. Now a permanent invariant in the committed suite.

subject: subscripted annotations were emitted FLAT, losing py_expression.depth
detail: `Optional[Dict[str, int]]` produced four sibling rows all at depth 0, because this grammar spells a subscripted annotation `generic_type` + `type_parameter` rather than `subscript`, and both fell through to the transparent fallback. `depth` is a frozen spine column and §2.6 notes that type-hierarchy.dl filters on depth == "0" to find the OUTERMOST reference, so a flat tree makes that filter select every nested argument too. It also left py_type_reference.pyExpressionLinkHash with no node to point at for the subscript itself — only for the bare name. Fixed: generic_type now yields kind=SUBSCRIPT with SUBSCRIPT_OBJECT / SUBSCRIPT_INDEX children, the same shape as `d[k]`, so `Optional[Dict[str, int]]` is now a depth-2 tree. Verified the anchors every deferred relation needs now exist: the STORE-context ATTRIBUTE_ACCESS with dottedPath=self.conn for py_field and py_field_write, the ASSIGNMENT_VALUE root for the write's RHS, the isinstance CALL under edgeRole=CONDITION for py_block narrowing, and the ANNOTATION-role subtree for py_type_reference.

Reproduced exactly and fixed. `class C(A,  # comment\n B)` emitted three py_type_base rows with the comment at MRO position 1 and B pushed to 2, and baseCount=3. Now 2 rows at positions 0,1 with names A,B. This is the third site of the same root cause after argument lists (f7f3081) and parameter lists (bdcfa3c), and the worst of the three because a base carries an MRO POSITION, so it silently corrupts C3 linearisation rather than just a count. Measured frequency across the 13,586-file corpus: 20 sites in 3 files, all tensorflow feature_column. Regression test added covering all three sites at once, including a line continuation in an argument list.

Reproduced and fixed. The construct is `member_type` — a dotted name in TYPE position whose left side is itself a type, as in `def f(v: A[int].Inner)`. The grammar gives it its own node rather than reusing `attribute`, so the generic walk visited its trailing identifier and invented a module binding for `Inner`. CPython's symtable says ['A','f','int']; we said ['A','Inner','f','int']; we now match. `splat_type` (`*Ts`) handled at the same time for the same reason. Same root-cause family as a4-037: an unrecognised node type traversed generically either invents an entity or drops a subtree.

a4-034 (no py_method row for any lambda, 15,725 missing) was fixed in b3f59b1, which postdates the 7946eb7 A4 audited. Lambdas now emit py_method with methodKind=LAMBDA and their own parameters, LAMBDA scopes resolve their ownerHash to that method, and calls inside a lambda body are attributed to the lambda rather than to the enclosing function. A4's diagnosis of why Gate 1 could not see it is exactly right and is why the fix also added a structural invariant: one LAMBDA method per LAMBDA scope.

Call-site and base resolution implemented. On src/test-data/python/linkage-sample: call sites 0/29 -> 22/29, type_base resolved locally 0/1 -> 1/1. All seven cases named in the brief now resolve, and to the CORRECT target, which matters more than the count: super().describe() inside Child.describe lands on models.Base.describe and NOT on Child.describe; Child.of('x') lands on models.Base.of through the inherited MRO; inner(items) lands on the exact nested def service.Service.run.<locals>.inner; build_pipeline and passthrough resolve cross-module to helpers. Corpus: 600 stdlib files, 45,506 call sites, 38.8% resolved overall — NONE 60.3%, SELF 47.7%, CLS 70.2%, SUPER 29.8%, NAME 24.1%, and 0% for ATTRIBUTE/CALL_RESULT/LITERAL/SUBSCRIPT, which all require receiver typing from the deferred relations.

subject: why resolution was 0%, and why it was only 55% after the first fix
detail: Two distinct bugs. (1) There was no resolution pass at all — every resolvedCalleeKind was written UNRESOLVED at construction and never revisited. (2) After adding the pass it reached only 16/29, because symtable emits a py_binding row for any name a scope MENTIONS, including one it only reads as GLOBAL_IMPLICIT. The scope-chain walk treated that row as a shadowing bind and stopped, so only ZERO-hop lookups succeeded: a nested def resolved, but a module-level function referenced from inside a function did not. Fixed with PyBindingRegistry.isBound() (isAssigned || isImported || isParameter), which is the DEF_BOUND question rather than the 'is mentioned' question. The same confusion had made every builtin unresolvable, since `sorted` has a mention row in every scope that calls it.

subject: over-resolution hazard found while implementing resolution
detail: A nested `def` carries its enclosing class in pyTypeLinkHash, so a naive 'methods of this type' lookup offered service.Service.run.<locals>.inner as a candidate for self.inner() — a target unreachable by that path. Added PyMethodRegistry.isClassBodyMember() (has a type AND no enclosing member) and filtered attribute lookup through it. Also excluded @overload stubs and bodyIsStub methods from lookup, per §2.7's rule that they are declarations and never call targets, which is what lets a name with two stubs plus one implementation resolve to the implementation rather than reading as ambiguous.

subject: Resolution gate — consistency invariant, no oracle needed
detail: Added to src/test/python-extractor-tests.ts and run over the sweep corpus. Both sides of each implication are relations the parser emits, and the expectation is recomputed independently from py_binding / py_type_base / py_method rather than from the linker, so the check cannot be satisfied by the linker agreeing with itself. Three rules: a bare name bound in the scope chain to a def/class must resolve to exactly that entity; self.N with exactly one declared target on the class closure must resolve to it; a base naming a class in the same module must have resolvedTypeLinkHash set to it with isResolvedLocally true. It asserts EQUALITY with the independently derived target, so over-resolution to a wrong target fails it just as under-resolution does. Result: 0 violations over 600 files / 45,506 call sites. This closes the hole A4 identified — Gate 1 compares scopes and bindings, which are identical whether resolution runs or not, and Gate 2 checks call-site structure, which was already correct, so 0% resolution showed green on both.

subject: isArgsKwargsPassthrough is DECLARES, not FORWARDS — A4 is right, and here is the number
detail: Answering A4's question. Intent per schema §2.7 c27 is DECLARES: 'both *args and **kwargs (2.8%). Marks where positional param-flow is provably unsound.' My implementation matches the schema (isVarArgs && hasKwArgs). The unsoundness claim is still correct under declares-semantics, and this is the part worth being precise about: the unsoundness is a property of the CALLEE'S SIGNATURE, not of its body — if a function declares *args then a caller's 5th positional argument has no named parameter to bind to, whether or not the body forwards anything. So the flag supports the claim it is documented to support. But A4 is right that the NAME says forwards, and that is a real trap for anyone reading the column rather than the schema. Measured over 1,500 stdlib files / 28,658 methods: 346 declare both, of which 239 (69.1%) forward both onward, 16 forward one, and 91 forward neither. So a forwards-reading of the 559 figure would be inflated by roughly 30%. Recommendation, and it is your call not mine: keep the column's declares-semantics (the schema and the unsoundness claim both depend on it) and either rename it toward 'declaresVarArgsAndKwargs' at the fact layer — names are not the frozen contract, column ORDER is — or add a separate forwards column in the second freeze. I have not widened this column's meaning and will not without a ruling.

subject: cross-module base resolution was 0% — one missing import shape cascaded into SUPER
detail: Confirmed A4's measurement and traced the cause. The join baseSimpleName -> py_import -> target module -> py_type was missing in two distinct ways. (1) resolveTypeBases ran ONLY in the per-module pass, and it deliberately skipped dotted bases on the grounds that a dotted prefix names something outside the module — correct for a single-module pass, wrong for the project pass, where `protocols.Protocol` names a sibling. 44 of 60 unresolved bases in asyncio were exactly that shape. (2) The bigger one: `from . import protocols` binds a MODULE, not a member of one, and my import model looked for `protocols` as a class or function inside the package, never found it, and gave up. Because sibling modules were then unreachable, every base spelled `protocols.Protocol` stayed unresolved, which in turn blocked super() and self.X on those classes — a single missing import shape produced the largest failure bucket downstream. Result on asyncio: py_type_base 39/99 -> 82/99, cross-module bases 0/43 -> 43/50 (the 7 remaining are genuinely external: threading.Thread, enum.Enum, code.InteractiveConsole). SUPER 26% -> 66.7%, SELF -> 92.7%.

subject: absolute intra-package imports failed when the analysis root is inside the package
detail: Module names are relative to the analysis root, so analysing .../email directly names modules `parser` and `message` while the source says `from email.parser import Parser`. Result: email had 0 of 132 imports resolved in-project. Now handled by progressively dropping leading segments and accepting a candidate only when exactly ONE module matches, so an ambiguous suffix resolves to nothing rather than to a guess. email: imports 0/132 -> 73/132, bases 90/109 -> 100/109. Worth stating as a usage note too: analysing from the repo root gives strictly better resolution than analysing from inside a package.

subject: transitive MRO implemented; sibling ambiguity now REFUSED, and the number went down
detail: Per instruction, transitive lookup within an inheritance CHAIN (nearest declaration wins, any depth — Lock -> _LoopBoundMixin two hops up) but sibling bases offering DIFFERENT targets are refused rather than linearised. Reporting the direction honestly: SUPER on asyncio went 55/72 -> 48/72 when I tightened this, because the earlier depth-first-first-wins had been claiming 7 targets that depended on a C3 linearisation I do not compute. 48 is the sound number and 55 contained guesses. Every remaining SUPER/SELF failure now has a stated cause: 11 SUPER + 8 SELF have a base OUTSIDE the analysis (opaque, could shadow); 7 SUPER + 2 SELF are sibling ambiguity (the _Proactor*Transport shape); 6 SUPER + 22 SELF name something declared nowhere in the reachable closure; 3 SELF have no explicit base so the target is on object.

subject: the analyzer OOMs on the full 13,586-file corpus
detail: Running the project analyzer over the entire stdlib plus site-packages exhausts the V8 heap: accumulate-then-export holds every row in memory, and py_expression alone is 11M rows there. This is inherent to the determinism requirement as currently implemented — a total order over the fact base needs the rows in hand before writing. Per-package and per-repo runs are unaffected (asyncio, email, xml, logging all complete comfortably), and the per-file test sweep is unaffected because it does not accumulate. Flagging rather than fixing: the fix is either streaming with an external sort or sharding by module, and both change the export contract, so it is a design call rather than a bug fix.

subject: resolution gate extended to cross-module bases
detail: The gate previously asserted base resolution only for same-module name matches, which is exactly why 0/43 cross-module bases passed it — the check could not see the gap it existed to guard. Now a base whose baseSimpleName names a py_type REACHABLE through this module's py_import rows must have resolvedTypeLinkHash set to that type with isResolvedLocally true. Gate result: 0 violations over 400 files / 26,391 call sites, alongside 0 Gate-1 and 0 Gate-2 disagreements.

Bisected as asked, and the bisect changed the fix. `class Mixed(Child, Sibling)` calling super().describe() now resolves to Child.describe, verified against CPython's Mixed.__mro__ = (Mixed, Child, Base, Sibling, object). BISECT RESULT: both COMMITTED versions returned UNRESOLVED (167c0bd refused on distinct-candidates; 3513360 refused on sibling ambiguity), so the variant A4 remembers working was an uncommitted intermediate that used first-hit depth-first. I reconstructed and ran it: it resolves Mixed correctly AND resolves `class D(B, C)` where `class B(A)`, `class C(A)` with A and C both declaring m to A.m — where CPython says C.m, because A sits in C's tail. So 'it used to work' was true for one shape and silently WRONG for another, which is why reverting would have been the wrong move. Also retracting my earlier claim that tightening this removed 7 'guesses': the tightening was itself over-strict, and real C3 recovers those cases correctly rather than refusing them.

subject: real C3 linearisation implemented, plus two provable shortcuts for when it fails
detail: Full C3 with the standard merge (take the head of the first sequence that appears in no other sequence's TAIL; null when none qualifies, mirroring CPython refusing to create the class), memoised per type. Three refinements were each forced by a measured over-refusal, and each is provable rather than heuristic. (1) A class is always FIRST in its own MRO, so a declaration on the class itself needs no linearisation and cannot be shadowed by an opaque base — requiring the MRO here refused 1,549 self.X calls across 400 files. (2) An explicit `object` base is the implicit root written longhand and is NOT opaque: its member set is fixed and entirely dunder, so it cannot be the target of an ordinary name — treating it as unknown blocked everything under `class X(object)`, including argparse.ArgumentParser. (3) When linearisation fails, what a claim actually needs is only the MRO PREFIX up to the declaring class. Under single inheritance that prefix is just the chain, so it is walkable without the rest; and with multiple bases, base 0's HEAD is still provably MRO index 1, because it could only be deferred if a later base inherited from it, which is exactly the inconsistent hierarchy CPython rejects. Result: gate violations 1549 -> 33 -> 3 -> 0, and per-file resolution 36.9% -> 43.4%.

subject: parameter and return annotations — what is emitted
detail: Answering the question about `def add(a: int, b: int) -> int`. Yes, both directions are captured. Per parameter: parameterTypeName is the annotation as written (`Optional[float]`, `Dict[str, str]`), parameterBaseType is it minus subscripts (`Optional`, `Dict`), paramKind distinguishes POSITIONAL_ONLY / POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD / KEYWORD_ONLY / VAR_POSITIONAL / VAR_KEYWORD plus the bare `/` and `*` markers as their own rows, hasDefault / defaultValueText / defaultValueKind carry the default, isMutableDefault fires on a list/dict/set/call default, and annotationIsString marks a string forward reference. Per method: returnTypeName holds the `-> X` text and detailedSignature reproduces the whole thing including annotations and defaults. Verified that a string annotation creates no phantom binding — `def f(x: "Node")` gives module bindings ['f','int'] matching CPython exactly, since PEP 563 aside, a quoted annotation is a literal and not a reference. The annotation EXPRESSION is also emitted as a py_expression subtree under edgeRole=ANNOTATION with correct depth, which is what the deferred py_type_reference will attach to.

subject: annotations named a custom type but linked to nothing
detail: For `def add(a: CustomTypeA, b: CustomTypeB) -> CustomTypeC` the parser recorded the annotation TEXT and nothing else: py_method_parameter.potentialQualifiedName was empty on every row, py_binding.declaredBaseType and potentialQualifiedName likewise, and there was no FK to the py_type at all. Same class of defect as the UNRESOLVED call sites — the answer is derivable, CustomTypeA is imported from an in-project module, and the engine cannot recover it because re-deriving a type from annotation TEXT is exactly what the schema forbids it to do. Now: potentialQualifiedName resolves to models.CustomTypeA and joins to the py_type hash, declaredBaseType is populated, and isAmbiguous is set when a wildcard import is in scope so the imprecision is a fact rather than a silence.

subject: py_expression.referencedEntityHash was empty — the type-reference link Java gets from java_type_reference
detail: A4/human asked what plays the role of Java's all-type-references.csv. py_type_reference is in the deferred eleven, so until it lands the frozen columns py_expression.referencedEntityKind / referencedEntityHash (c14/c15) are where a USE of a type reaches the type's hash — and I was leaving both empty. Now populated for every NAME_REFERENCE that resolves to an in-project class or function, via the same scope-chain machinery as call-site resolution. This matters most for NESTED annotations: `y: Optional[CustomTypeB]` resolves its BASE to Optional, which is external, so potentialQualifiedName is legitimately empty — but the inner CustomTypeB is a NAME_REFERENCE at depth 1 in the annotation subtree and now carries a direct one-hop FK to models.CustomTypeB. Worth recording WHY the obvious alternative fails: joining through bindingLinkHash works only at module scope, because inside a class or method the binding is the LOCAL reference row rather than the module-level import that defined the name, so that join dead-ends precisely where it is most needed.

subject: recommend UN-DEFERRING py_type_reference — three things the spine cannot express
detail: With potentialQualifiedName and referencedEntityHash now populated, a type USE reaches a type HASH, so the immediate question is answered. But three things py_type_reference carries have no home in the frozen spine and are genuinely lost today, and they are the reasons Java has the relation as its own CSV. (1) CONTEXT: py_expression cannot say whether a type use is a METHOD_PARAM, METHOD_RETURN, FIELD_TYPE, ISINSTANCE_TYPE, EXCEPT_TYPE or CAST_TARGET — the enum for that is py_type_reference.context (c1), and edgeRole only distinguishes ANNOTATION from the rest. (2) RETURN TYPES have nowhere to be resolved: py_method has returnTypeName (c12) as text and no potentialQualifiedName counterpart, so `-> CustomTypeC` is resolvable only through the annotation EXPRESSION, not from the method row. (3) The generic STRUCTURE — parentReferenceHash, position, depth, isOptional — which §2.6 notes type-hierarchy.dl filters on. I now emit the annotation expression subtree with correct nesting and depth so a future py_type_reference can attach 1:1, and I am NOT emitting the relation, per the freeze. Recommending it for the second freeze, or earlier if the engine needs context/return resolution before then. Your call.

subject: a parameter row could not enumerate the N types its annotation references
detail: Follow-up to the annotation work, and the sharper form of the same question. py_method_parameter has ONE potentialQualifiedName slot, so `Dict[TypeA, TypeB]` cannot be expressed there at all — it resolves the BASE, `Dict`, which is external, leaving the row saying nothing about TypeA or TypeB. The N entries did exist in the py_expression annotation subtree, one referencedEntityHash each, but there was NO route from the parameter row to them: pyExpressionLinkHash is designated for the DEFAULT value (§2.8 c19), and joining by span would be span-matching, which the schema forbids. Fixed by making a parameter's annotation subtree OWNED BY THE PARAMETER — expressionOwnerKind=METHOD_PARAMETER, which is in the frozen enum for exactly this and which I had been setting to METHOD. Now enumerable by one join: Dict[TypeA, TypeB] -> [TypeA, TypeB]; Dict[TypeA, List[Optional[TypeB]]] -> [TypeA, TypeB]; Union[TypeA, TypeB] -> [TypeA, TypeB]; PEP 604 `TypeA | TypeB` -> [TypeA, TypeB] (a BINARY_OPERATION, not a subscript); Callable[[TypeA, TypeB], TypeC] -> [TypeA, TypeB, TypeC] with the arguments a level deeper inside a LIST. Permanent test covers all five nesting shapes. Traceability invariant extended so METHOD_PARAMETER resolves to a method through the parameter's own FK.

subject: restating the py_type_reference case now that the workaround is visible
detail: The N-per-annotation requirement is now met through py_expression ownership, so nothing is LOST. But it is worth being explicit that this is a workaround for a missing relation rather than the intended design, because the shape of the workaround shows what the relation is for. Enumerating a parameter's types now means: filter py_expression on expressionOwnerHash = the parameter AND referencedEntityKind = TYPE. With py_type_reference it would be: select from py_type_reference where typeReferenceOwnerHash = the parameter — one relation, with context (METHOD_PARAM vs METHOD_RETURN vs ISINSTANCE_TYPE), position, depth, parentReferenceHash and isOptional carried as columns instead of inferred from the expression tree's shape. Two things still have no expression: a resolved RETURN type (py_method.returnTypeName is text with no potentialQualifiedName counterpart, so `-> TypeC` is reachable only through the expression tree, never from the method row), and the CONTEXT of a type use. Recommendation unchanged: un-defer py_type_reference. It attaches 1:1 to the annotation subtree I already emit, so it needs no spine change.

subject: py_type_reference IMPLEMENTED — first of the deferred eleven, on explicit direction
detail: Flagging clearly because it crosses the freeze boundary I was told to hold: the standing instruction was 'the other 11 relations are deferred — do not emit them.' The human then specified the required design directly ('first entry for Dict and then another 2 linking to the parent as the hash of the typereference of dict with index, that is how it is done in java'), so I implemented it to §2.6 exactly — 25 columns in frozen order, PK = md5(typeReferenceOwnerHash || context || parentReferenceHash || position || depth || completeTypeName || startLine), exported as all-python-type-references.csv. The 262-column spine is UNTOUCHED: the test suite now keeps SPINE_ARITY (10 relations, 262) separate from DEFERRED_ARITY so the schema-document check still verifies 262 rather than reporting 287 and reading as drift. If this was not the intent, it is one commit to revert and no spine column changes with it.

subject: why a nested tree was the only way to express a composite annotation
detail: The requirement, restated because it is the justification for the relation: `Dict[TypeA, TypeB]` references three types that are RELATED to each other, and every spine slot holds one value. py_method_parameter.potentialQualifiedName resolves the BASE only, so it recorded `Dict` (external, hence empty) and said nothing about TypeA or TypeB. The tree now emits one row per reference with parentReferenceHash + position + depth, so `Dict[TypeA, List[Optional[TypeB]]]` yields the path Dict > List > Optional > TypeB at depths 0-3 with positions distinguishing siblings. NOTE the shape differs deliberately from the py_expression tree over the same text: there SUBSCRIPT is a node and Dict is its first child, whereas here Dict IS the depth-0 reference and the arguments are its children — which is what java_type_reference does, and what makes 'the type being parameterised' and 'its parameters' a parent/child pair rather than siblings. Contexts collected: METHOD_PARAM, METHOD_RETURN (which had NO home on the spine at all), BASE_CLASS, METACLASS, VARIABLE_ANNOTATION, and GENERIC_ARGUMENT for everything nested. Callable[[A, B], R] flattens the bracketed parameter list, since it is not itself a type. isOptional is set for Optional[X] and for any union with a None member. Verified at scale on asyncio: 116 references, 0 dangling parents, depths 0-3.

Wired. The twin rows existed on both sides — the type-reference row already carried typeReferenceOwnerHash pointing AT the base — but §2.5 c9, the reverse link, was never set, and type-hierarchy.dl traverses base -> type_reference, so a ported Java rule found nothing. Now populated for every base that NAMES a type: positional bases and metaclass=. A non-metaclass keyword such as `total=False` on a TypedDict correctly gets none, because it names a value rather than a type — 10/11 on a fixture covering plain, dotted, generic, mixin, metaclass and TypedDict bases. Only the DEPTH-0 reference is the twin: a nested argument such as the T in `class Box(Generic[T])` shares the owner but is not the base's own reference.

subject: inverse FK assertion added — the blind spot A4 named
detail: A4's point was the important one: FK integrity reported 0 orphans across 2,331 references BECAUSE an empty FK is skipped by orphan checking, so a designed-but-never-populated link looks healthy. The new assertion is the inverse, exactly as specified: every py_type_base row that names a type must have pyTypeReferenceLinkHash set, it must resolve, its context must be BASE_CLASS (or METACLASS for a metaclass row), its typeName must equal the base's baseSimpleName, and it must point back at that base row. It immediately caught a SECOND defect: baseSimpleName was being filled for COMPUTED bases — `class _Method(_namedtuple('_Method', ...))` and `class _swapped_meta(type(Structure))` were reporting baseSimpleName=_namedtuple and =type. §2.5 c3 says '"" if not name-shaped', and a call is not; returning the callee's name would claim the class inherits from _namedtuple rather than from whatever the call returned, which a name->type resolver would then resolve to the wrong class. Fixed.

subject: inheritance and polymorphism adjudicated against CPython at runtime
detail: Built a third-source check for the thing that most needed it: for every class, compare my C3 linearisation against cls.__mro__, and for every callable visible on a class compare my override resolution against CPython's own attribute lookup. This is the interpreter answering, not a second static implementation. Over 700 stdlib modules (128 unjudged because importing them fails): MRO ORDER 581/581 = 100%; OVERRIDE RESOLUTION 10,893/10,900 = 99.9% where the parser has an answer, with 0 wrong answers on 300 files and 7 on 700. Three classes of case are excluded as not adjudicable by runtime introspection, each for a stated reason rather than convenience: a class with a COMPUTED base, because `class _Method(_namedtuple('_Method',...))` makes CPython's MRO contain a dynamically created class with the same module AND name as its subclass; a class with a custom METACLASS, because `class IntEnum(int, Enum)` has an EMPTY body in source yet EnumMeta injects __new__, __repr__ and _generate_next_value_ into its __dict__, so CPython names IntEnum as the declaring class for methods written nowhere; and the 3,917 'missing' answers, which are all one pattern.

subject: class-body method ALIASES are invisible without py_field
detail: Every remaining override disagreement is one pattern: a class-body assignment binding a callable, which shadows an inherited method. `__str__ = __unicode__` (lib2to3/pytree.py), `getstate = setstate = _notimplemented` (random.py), `__reduce__ = _IPAddressBase.__reduce__` (ipaddress.py), and the `__rand__ = __and__` family in _collections_abc.py. Two consequences, and the split matters: 3,917 cases where the name exists ONLY as an alias, so the parser has no answer and correctly claims none; and 7 cases where the name also exists as a real def further up the chain, so the parser resolves to the inherited def while CPython resolves to the local alias — 7 wrong out of 10,900. A class attribute bound to a callable is py_field territory, which is deferred, so this cannot be fixed inside the current relation set. Recording it as the cost of that deferral rather than as an open parser bug.

subject: v7 amendment to py_expression — APPROVED from the implementation side
detail: Signing off on folding py_type_inference into four appended py_expression columns (c33-c36). The amendment is safe by CONSTRUCTION rather than by inspection, which is the part worth stating: the PK is built from c0-c32 only, so appending cannot move a single hash, and svc/PK shifting to c37/c38 is what 'append only, hash last' does on every append. Implemented and verified — 39 columns emitted, output still byte-identical across runs, all 18 fixtures clean on all three gates. I also agree with the reasoning, not just the mechanics: every inference a PARSER may make really is 1:1 with one node, and `x = 3; x = "hi"` really is two singly-typed ASSIGNMENT_VALUE nodes. The union is a join over the binding. Spine is now 266, and the schema-document ratchet caught the change on the first run after the append, which is what it is for.

subject: py_field + py_field_position un-deferred and emitted
detail: Emitting 29-column py_field and 3-column py_field_position. py_field_write is NOT emitted, per §2.10 — the write facts are already on py_expression and the only thing it added was a join key, so the join is performed as a resolution rule instead and written to the polymorphic referencedEntityKind/referencedEntityHash pair. Ten origins are distinguished because the mechanism matters: a class-body assign, a bare annotation, a self-assign, an augmented self-assign, a __slots__ entry, a dataclass field, a NamedTuple field, a TypedDict key, an enum member, and a constant-name setattr. Attribute names are MANGLED, matching CPython: self.__x inside class C stores _C__x, so `name` equals the runtime __dict__ key and matches what py_binding already does; storing __x would let a reference from a different class match this field, which at runtime raises AttributeError. bindingLinkHash is populated for class-body fields and deliberately EMPTY for self.* — §2.9 c25's point, and not an omission: CPython's symtable records `self` and records the attribute nowhere at all.

subject: ATTRIBUTE receiver resolution 0% -> 16.4%, and exactly why
detail: On asyncio: ATTRIBUTE went 0/518 to 85/518, then 81/518 after a soundness guard removed 4 unsound claims. Diagnosed before implementing rather than after: of 510 unresolved sites, 387 ALREADY FOUND THE FIELD and were blocked only on the field's TYPE — so the gap really was a missing fact, not a missing rule, which is what the forecast said. Breakdown of the blockers matched it closely: 164 initialised from a NAME (parameter or local), 143 from a literal, 104 no field at all, ~50 from a stdlib or dotted constructor. Three grounds are now admitted for an attribute's type, and each refuses rather than guesses: an ANNOTATION; a CONSTRUCTOR call whose name resolves to a class in the declaring module; and a PARAMETER whose annotation types what was passed in (self._loop = loop). A field annotation resolves in the namespace of the module that DECLARES it, not the one calling through it — `self.q: Queue` means whatever Queue meant where the class was written — so the name->type map is built per module and the attribute's type is settled before any cross-module call site consults it.

subject: builtin receiver resolution, with the method set taken from CPython
detail: An attribute known to hold a builtin now resolves calls on it: self._buf = bytearray() then self._buf.extend(d) reaches bytearray.extend, reported as BUILTIN with an empty hash — the same treatment a bare len(x) already gets, since no py_method row exists for a builtin. The method sets are GENERATED from CPython 3.10.4 itself (dir(list) and friends), not hand-written, and the membership test is the whole point: without it, self._items = [] followed by self._items.frobnicate() would be reported as a builtin call, which is wrong AND would launder a real bug in the analysed code into a fact. Two guards on top. `{}` is a dict and `{1}` is a set — same opening brace, and they share almost no methods, so the top-level colon decides rather than a coin flip. And an attribute written with two DIFFERENT builtin types is not either of them: self.result = [] in one method and self.result = None in another sets isAmbiguous (c4, which exists for exactly this) and refuses. That guard cost 4 of 85 claims on asyncio, which is the right direction of trade.

subject: oracle defect #6 — receiverKind reports a receiver where none exists
detail: 4 disagreements on the 400-file sweep, and the oracle is wrong in both shapes. (1) configparser.py:553,555 — `match.group(1)` inside LegacyInterpolation._interpolation_replace. Oracle says receiverKind=SELF; the method is a @staticmethod, so its first parameter is an ordinary argument and there is no receiver. Verified at runtime: isinstance(LegacyInterpolation.__dict__['_interpolation_replace'], staticmethod) is True. (2) copyreg.py:101,107 — `cls.__new__(cls, *args)` inside __newobj__. Oracle says CLS; __newobj__ is a MODULE-LEVEL function whose first parameter merely happens to be named cls. Verified: copyreg.__newobj__.__qualname__ == '__newobj__'. Both look like receiver detection keyed on the first parameter's name or position without checking staticmethod-ness or whether the function is in a class at all. Parser answer is NAME in all four. Not bending the parser to match.

subject: my own '400/400 fully clean' was measured on a stale tool — real figure was 377/400
detail: Correcting a number I reported earlier today. Re-running the full sweep after this change showed 377/400, and my first instinct was that I had regressed something. I checked against HEAD before claiming either way: both problem classes reproduce at HEAD, so this change introduced neither. The 55 'FN_SPURIOUS <lambda>' were a defect in MY OWN comparison tool, not the parser — the oracle's ast dump enumerates `def`s only and reports ZERO lambdas (ast.py has 19 by ast.walk, the dump lists none), so every lambda py_method row looked spurious the moment lambdas started being emitted (a4-034), and the tool was never updated. Lambda coverage is not lost by excluding them from a `def`-shape check, because Gate 1 already verifies it EXACTLY: symtable emits a block per lambda and those are compared name-for-name. Sweep is now 398/400, with the remaining 4 being the oracle defect above. The lesson I am recording against myself: a green number from a tool that has drifted from the parser is worth less than no number, and I should re-derive rather than re-quote.

subject: the analyzer filed a parser CRASH as READ_ERROR and still reported success
detail: Found while wiring py_field: a bug in my new stage threw on every file, and the analyzer caught it, recorded SkippedFileReason.READ_ERROR, and completed with an EMPTY py_field CSV and no non-zero exit. My own measurement script then failed on the empty file, which is the only reason I noticed. This is the same blind spot A4 identified for empty FKs, in a different place: a defect disguised as an environmental condition. Fixed two ways. A new SkippedFileReason.EXTRACTION_ERROR distinguishes 'the parser failed', which is always a bug, from 'the file could not be read', which is nobody's; and PythonAnalysisSummary now carries extractionErrors separately from filesRejected, because a caller that treats them alike cannot tell a clean run from a parser that crashed on every file. A rejected file is a decision. An extraction error is a defect. Reporting them in one bucket is how the first can hide the second.

subject: CALL_RESULT resolution — no relation needed, as forecast
detail: Implemented and verified. Three grounds, and two of the three need no annotation at all: `Conn().send()` resolves because calling a CLASS always yields an instance of it; `self._get_loop().create_future()` resolves through the MRO to the inner method, which was 6 of asyncio's 12 CALL_RESULT sites and the shape my first regex missed; and `make_pool().acquire()` resolves through a `-> Pool` return annotation. Refusals are deliberate: an unannotated factory could return anything, and `self.pool.all().append()` is three hops through List[Conn], where each extra hop compounds the chance of a wrong answer. Verified 11 of 12 on a purpose-built scratch case with both refusals correct.

subject: the stdlib annotates 0.1% of parameters and 0.0% of returns — this reframes every resolution number we have quoted
detail: Measured over the same 400 files: 5 of 8,585 parameters carry an annotation, and 2 of 7,049 functions carry a return type. So annotation-driven resolution has essentially NO FUEL in this corpus, and the resolution rates we have been quoting — mine and A4's — are measuring the corpus as much as the parser. Concrete evidence: the parameter-flow and factory-return rules are correct and verified 11/12 on a typed scratch case, and they moved the stdlib numbers by ZERO, because there is nothing for them to read. What the stdlib's remaining ATTRIBUTE resolutions come from is constructor initialisers and builtin literals, not annotations. Recommendation, for the human rather than for me to decide: the acceptance corpus should include at least one MODERN TYPED codebase, or we will keep tuning against the least favourable input in existence and reporting it as the parser's ceiling. A 43% figure on 0.1%-annotated code and a 43% figure on fully annotated code mean completely different things about the same parser.

subject: what is still missing, ranked by what it blocks, with counts
detail: Emitting 13 of v7's 19 relations. Remaining six, honestly ranked. (1) py_block — 13,108 instances in 400 files (If 9,988, For 1,291, Try 1,177, While 421, With 231). Carries isinstance narrowing and reachability; the largest genuinely-missing structure. (2) py_decorator + py_decorator_argument — and here the stdlib measurement argues AGAINST urgency rather than for it: only 3.7% of stdlib declarations are decorated (321 of 8,622) and the top four are property/classmethod/abstractmethod/staticmethod, all of which methodKind ALREADY carries, with just 12 decorator arguments in total. The value is in framework code, where @app.route and auth decorators live, and the stdlib cannot measure that — so this is a decision about target corpus, not a gap I can size honestly from here. (3) py_comment and (4) py_parse_gap — auxiliary; parse gaps matter only for malformed input, which the 32,767-char workaround already prevents on valid files. (5) py_type_parameter — PEP 695, genuinely N/A on 3.10. What is NOT missing: local variables are complete (7,662/7,663 name references carry bindingLinkHash, and py_binding IS the local-variable table), and field/attribute links are now complete on both sides.

subject: DOTTED bases do not resolve — `class T(unittest.TestCase)` — and it caps SELF resolution
detail: Found while measuring coverage across 18 packages, not by reading code. In unittest, py_type_base resolves 53/522 = 10.2%, and the top unresolved base is `unittest.TestCase` with 244 occurrences. The consequence is much larger than the base rows themselves: 3,201 SELF call sites in unittest are UNRESOLVED, and the top callees are assertEqual (1,305), assertRaises (544), assertIn (174) — every one of which is declared on TestCase and reachable by MRO the moment the base resolves. That is why aggregate SELF reads 30.9% while asyncio alone reads 93.3%: the spread is not noise, it is this one defect. Cause: resolveTypeBases deliberately skips any base whose dotted path contains a '.', on the correct reasoning that `pkg.mod.Cls` names something outside the module even when its last segment collides with a local class — but the project pass only handles the `from . import x` member-module form, never `import unittest` followed by `unittest.TestCase`. Fixing the dotted-base join is now the highest-value resolution work left, ahead of any new relation.

subject: the ATTRIBUTE forecast, checked against measured reality on the same 400 files
detail: Re-ran the forecast's own decomposition after implementing py_field. The bucket SIZING was accurate — actual vs forecast: constructor 168 vs 147, literal 373 vs 323, param-or-local 382 vs 408, complex 217 vs 303, never-assigned 241 vs 291. The headline was BEATEN: ATTRIBUTE went 0/2,537 to 1,078/2,537 = 42.5% against a ~32% forecast. But the composition is not what was predicted, and that matters more than the number. Only 198 of the 1,078 are self-rooted; the other 880 come from receivers the forecast did not model at all — a receiver whose head names an imported module, reported IMPORTED. The self-rooted subset alone is 198/1,381 = 14.3%, BELOW the ~32% forecast. One bucket is flatly wrong, and it is the largest: 'param or local, 408 sites, unblocked by arg->param flow (already wired)' delivered 0/382 = 0.0%. The flow is implemented and verified 11/12 on annotated code — it reads nothing here because the stdlib annotates 0.1% of parameters. One bucket beat its forecast: 'never assigned in class' was called genuinely unresolvable, and 7/241 resolved, because the field lookup walks the MRO and finds attributes declared in a base.

subject: the Gate 2 caveat is right, and I now have a concrete instance of it
detail: Endorsing the arbiter's point that Gate 1 and Gate 2 must not be folded into one number: symtable computes scopes by a different algorithm in a different language, while Gate 2 is a second implementation sharing an author with the harness, so it detects 'adjudicate this', not 'you are correct'. I hit exactly that failure mode this week and it is worth recording as evidence rather than agreement. My Gate 2 comparison reported 55 spurious lambdas across 400 files. The oracle's ast dump enumerates defs only and reports ZERO lambdas; the parser was right, CPython's own ast agreed with the parser, and the check had simply never been updated after lambdas started being emitted. A shared-author check went green for months and then went red for a reason that had nothing to do with the parser. That is the blind spot named, observed in the wild.

subject: SELF was plumbing, exactly as called — 10.5% to 96.7% on unittest
detail: The arbiter's ranking was right and worth acting on immediately: SELF outranks ATTRIBUTE by 2.5x in volume and needed no missing relation. It was a chain of THREE bugs, each hiding the next, and none of them analysis. (1) Module qualified names were derived from the path relative to rootDir, so analysing .../python3.10/unittest named its modules `case`, `loader` and `__init__` — meaning no module was called `unittest`, `class T(unittest.TestCase)` could never join, and `__init__` was not even unique across packages. Now the name is derived by walking up while __init__.py is present, which is Python's own rule and makes the name independent of where analysis started. (2) `__init__.py` IS its package, but relative-import resolution popped a segment for it as though it were a submodule, so every `from .case import TestCase` re-export in a package __init__ failed — which is precisely where re-exports live. (3) Dotted bases were skipped outright. Result on unittest: type_base 10.2% -> 63.4%, SELF 10.5% -> 96.7%, total 38.0% -> 67.6%. Across 18 packages, concrete call-graph edges went 19.6% -> 27.0%.

subject: precision — the companion metric, and it changes my own headline
detail: Agreed the resolution rate alone is half a number, so here is the other half. Candidates per resolved site is 1 BY CONSTRUCTION: resolvedCalleeHash is a single column, so the relation cannot express a fan-out and the fan-to-everything strategy is not available to score against. But the 42.1% headline was still inflated, and by my own reporting rather than by fanning. Splitting resolved rows by whether they carry a HASH: concrete call-graph edge 27.0%, kind-only with an empty hash (BUILTIN/IMPORTED) 22.5%, unresolved 50.5%. The kind-only rows are honest facts — the target is outside the analysis, so a hash would be invented — but they are not call-graph edges and should never have been summed with rows that are. Per receiver, edge-only: SELF 59.1%, SUPER 64.5%, CLS 85.4%, NONE 35.9%, CALL_RESULT 9.8%, ATTRIBUTE 2.3%, NAME 2.0%. ATTRIBUTE is the correction that matters: I reported 0 -> 26.7% and the call-graph-edge figure is 0 -> 2.3%. The rest is IMPORTED — receivers whose head names an imported module — which py_field had nothing to do with.

subject: two errors of mine the arbiter caught, and one stale item in their table
detail: (1) Sum integrity: the arbiter is right that the rows did not sum, and it was purely my reporting. The tool emitted all 10 receiver kinds summing exactly to 19,273/45,794; I truncated to 6 rows when writing the summary and kept the full TOTAL, which manufactured a 24/750 phantom. subject: py_field_position is now 1:1, and my reasoning for skipping SELF_ASSIGN was wrong
detail: Fixed, and the arbiter's argument was decisive. I had given positions only to class-body declarations, reasoning that a self.x recovered from a method body has no declaration order to report. That inverted the relation's purpose: Python's constructor-assigned fields are almost all SELF_ASSIGN, so the rows I skipped were exactly the ones a rule matching constructor arguments to fields needs — 2 rows for 11 fields against Java's 6,875/6,875. Now every field gets a position, in the order the class actually establishes its attributes: class-body declarations first in declaration order, then method-recovered attributes in first-write order. For a @dataclass that is exactly the generated __init__ signature; for a hand-written __init__ it is the order the attributes come into existence, which is the closest true statement available and, unlike a line number, stable under reformatting.

subject: dotted nested type references resolve, including forward references
detail: Fixed 0/5. Resolution now walks segments instead of refusing dotted names, via an index from every dotted SUFFIX of a type's qualified name to that type, with collisions mapped to null so an ambiguous short name refuses while the longer unambiguous one still resolves. `TopOne.Inner` and `TopOne.Inner.Deepest` both resolve in the same file. Single-segment forward references already worked, which is why this only showed up in the dotted case.

subject: the 96.7% / 21.4% gap is a METRIC difference, and A4's metric is the correct one
detail: Reconciled exactly rather than argued. On asyncio, counting resolvedCalleeKind != UNRESOLVED gives 1,323/2,977; counting a non-empty resolvedCalleeHash gives 637/2,977 — A4's figure to the row. Their SELF (447/479) and SUPER (55/72) match mine precisely, which is what identified the difference: the divergence is entirely in NAME and ATTRIBUTE, where every one of my 'resolutions' was IMPORTED or BUILTIN with an EMPTY hash.
